text: How do you raise a Swami Vivekananda? Perhaps it takes two hands, pulling in different directions — a father who loved the world, and a mother who lived for God.

His father, Viswanath Datta, was an attorney of the High Court of Calcutta — a man of the world, and fully at ease in it. He was versed in English and in Persian, and loved to recite the poetry of Hafiz and the Bible, certain that both held truths unmatched by anything else men had written. He earned well, he travelled, he kept a fine table, and he enjoyed his life.

Yet beneath that worldly ease lay a large heart. He gave freely — even to fallen relatives, some of them lost to drink. When Naren once objected, his father told him that only one who has seen the depths of human suffering can feel for those who try to forget their sorrow. Compassion, the boy learnt, need not wear the robes of a saint.

From his father, Naren learnt discipline — and a way of seeing. Once, when the boy demanded to know what his father had done for him, the reply was only: 'Go and look at yourself in the mirror.' And when Naren asked how he should carry himself in the world, his father gave him five words that would steady him for life: 'Never show surprise at anything.' From this man he learnt to seize the heart of a matter, and to meet palaces and poverty alike, unshaken.

His mother, Bhuvaneswari Devi, was cast in another mould. Regal, gracious, she belonged to the old tradition of Hindu womanhood. She ran a large household, yet carried within her a deep stillness — a calm resignation to God that commanded the respect of all around her. She was the refuge of the poor. And she had committed vast portions of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata to memory.

It was she who first taught him — the Bengali alphabet, his earliest English words, and the great stories of the epics. And she gave him something deeper still. When he once came home wronged, she told him to hold to the truth, whatever it cost him, and never, under any circumstance, to abandon it. Years later, he would say: 'I am indebted to my mother for whatever knowledge I have acquired.'

So two hands shaped him. From his father — reason, breadth, and an unshakable calm. From his mother — faith, truth, and the nearness of God. The thinker and the devotee would live within the same man.

But a boy so richly made could not be easily contained. He was restless, and fearless, already drawn to the wandering monks who passed his door. Next — the child who would not be tamed, and the strange light he saw each night before sleep.
